prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy with the IceCube observatory

statement.case_for: This is a discovery that nature handed us rather than one that theory predicted. IceCube found a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos well above 5 sigma in 2013, and the 2017 alert and archival data tied neutrinos to the blazar TXS 0506+056. The 2022 NGC 1068 evidence and the 2023 Galactic-plane map came from independent analyses, so the result is not resting on a single claim. It opens a new observational window on the cosmic-ray accelerators and on the most extreme environments in the universe, and the Committee has only touched neutrino astronomy through Davis and Koshiba (solar and supernova neutrinos). The two names are defensible: Halzen conceived the cubic-kilometre ice detector and drove it through AMANDA to IceCube, and Karle was central to building the detector and the discovery analysis. I put discoveries first and people second, and this is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new window opening.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is attribution. IceCube is a large collaboration, and a prize to two people understates the roles of AMANDA-era colleagues and of DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES, whose work established that the concept could work. Source identification is also thin: only TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are individually significant, and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is still open. A second reservation is that B015 has by far the broadest opening support (all eight of us ranked it) and the cleanest two-person credit, so a prize that is easier to defend in every respect may well be the sensible choice.

responses.point: Olsson ranks IceCube fourth and worries that two individuals cannot fairly represent a large-collaboration discovery, that the early proposers are missing from the credit, and that independent confirmation from a second detector is limited.
responses.response: I take the attribution worry seriously and cannot dismiss it, but I think it is weaker here than for the pulsar-timing arrays, where no individual is pivotal. Halzen's role as the person who insisted on the ice-based design and carried it for three decades is not seriously contested, and Karle's role in the discovery analysis is documented. On confirmation, the diffuse flux does not rest on one analysis: several event channels (starting events, upgoing muons, cascades) give consistent fluxes within one detector, and the KM3NeT event adds context. I accept that a second large detector would make me more comfortable about sources, but not about the flux, which is the discovery we would be crediting.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first for its clear idea, decisive experiment and thorough control of systematics, with several independent laboratories reproducing it and the redefinition of the second near.
responses.response: I agree that B015 is solid, and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is about kind rather than quality. The lattice clock is a magnificent refinement of a measurement whose basic physics, the frequency comb and ion clocks, the Committee honoured in 2005 and 2012, and you yourself say it may be seen as an extended programme of engineering improvements. A new window on the universe is a different order of discovery than another order of magnitude in precision. If the redefinition of the second goes through, the case for Katori and Ye gets stronger, which is an argument for it as the clear fallback, not for putting it ahead of IceCube today.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators, the quantum spin Hall effect and the quantum anomalous Hall effect first, as a case where theory and experiment reinforced each other, fully mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the quality of the theory-experiment pairing, and I put the topological-insulator story second on my own ballot. My difficulty is the credit. Your three names leave out Mele, who co-authored the Kane-Mele papers, and Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal sit outside the list, with Zhang deceased. B003 and B018 split the same history in two ways, and nothing in the opening ballots tells me which cut is right. Xue's quantum anomalous Hall result is a real experimental landmark, but it is a distinct line from the quantum spin Hall effect and I would not want to merge them under one citation just to fit three seats.

responses.point: Pearce also ranks IceCube first, as a new observational window built by instrument builders, and has the diffuse flux well above 5 sigma, with NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane as supporting evidence.
responses.response: We agree on the core, but I would sharpen one point. The prize should be framed around the diffuse astrophysical flux and neutrino astronomy as such, not around source identification, which is still incomplete. A citation tied to TXS 0506+056 would invite precisely the criticism that the sources are not yet understood. Your note on DUMAND proposers is fair, but the credited pair is what we can defend, and I would rather state plainly in the citation that this is the opening of a field.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee will accept two names from a collaboration of hundreds, and how to handle the AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES history.
Whether the sources of the bulk of the diffuse flux will be resolved soon; a prize this year could look slightly early on the source side.
Whether B015 should win simply because eight of eight members ranked it and it has the cleanest credit, and whether the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait or to act.
Which cut of the topological-insulator credit (B003 or B018) is the right one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: my connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch any shortlisted candidate. Nothing in the profile ties me personally to the IceCube credited names.
